The same decoupling carries over to wide EP, where one engine spans an EP group of several nodes and attention runs with ADP. Under wide EP, the two phases use groups of different sizes and different communication kernels. SGLang, for example, evaluates prefill on 4-node groups with kernels built for throughput, and decode on 9-node groups with low-latency kernels captured in CUDA graphs [61]. phase switch therefore moves node from group of one phase to group of the other. Elastic EP performs such move without restart [3], but it transfers weights: when vLLM grows DeepSeek-V4-Pro group from 16 to 20 GB200 GPUs, the scale-up takes 92 in total to transfer weights, warm up, and capture CUDA graphs [2]. Evolving Infra avoids most of this weight transfer by again holding the union of what both groups need. Every node already holds the non-expert weights. For the experts, each group keeps two copies of every expert on different nodes, so each GPU holds twice its share. node can then leave group without taking away the last copy of any expert, and it can join any group at least half as large as its old one by serving experts that it already holds. For GLM-5.2 with NVFP4 experts, the second copy takes 7% of B200 memory in 4-node group and 3% in 9-node group. Nor does move reload kernels, because one engine can load the kernels of both phases, as the auto mode of SGLang does [61]. D.5 Comparison with Agent-aware Routers ThunderAgent [23] pauses agents to prevent KV-cache thrashing (Appendix A.4). Section 3.3 instead attributes the KV reuse that existing systems lose to where they place requests and which KV they evict. This subsection tests which explanation holds on GB300 nodes by comparing ThunderAgent with cache-aware routing and Evolving Infra. 34 Table D.4: KV capacity does not limit serving on GB300 nodes. We serve the Claude Code trace with 126 concurrent agents on 36 GB300 GPUs with GLM-5.2, which uses DSA (Appendix B.2). All three configurations keep the split at 4P5D (Table D.4). The first two run the SGLang engines of our baselines (Section 6.1), which evict host memory in LRU order, and differ only in how they choose the prefill node. Each of their prefill nodes caches up to 2.06 million tokens of KV in GPU memory and 8.25 million tokens in host memory, which holds one copy per node (Appendix A.5). For cache-aware routing, we reimplement the policy of the SGLang Model Gateway [58]. For ThunderAgent, we port the program scheduler that Dynamo ships as router plugin [23, 40] and keep its default thresholds. Since the plugin targets aggregated serving, we apply it to the choice of the prefill node and count host memory in the capacity of node. ThunderAgent pauses agents that wait for tools once the contexts of the active agents on node exceed 95% of this capacity. The harness marks the last request of each agent, so ThunderAgent releases finished agents at once. The Evolving Infra configuration is the run with fixed split in Section 6.4. We score minutes 30 to 85 of each run, and each configuration runs once. Results. ThunderAgent pauses no request (Table D.4): by its own estimate, the active agents on prefill node need at most 86% of its KV capacity (76% on average), below its 95% threshold, since the deduplicated host tier absorbs thrashing (Appendix A.5). It thus performs like cache-aware routing, with 2.6% versus 2.4% lost KV reuse, 0.95 the throughput, and 1.14 the mean TTFT. With the same split and host-memory ratio, Evolving Infra achieves 1.35 the throughput and 0.29 the mean TTFT of cache-aware routing and loses only 0.7% of the KV reuse, because its prefill nodes fetch KV from any node that holds it (Section 4.2) and evict first the copies that no active branch references (Section 4.3). Its higher TPOT coincides with larger decode batches, and this comparison does not separate the effects of routing and the data plane. On GB300 nodes, KV reuse therefore depends on where KV resides and which copies host memory keeps, not on KV capacity (Section 3.3). D.6 Async KV Fetching When prefill node fetches KV from host memory, it restores the KV into GPU memory and broadcasts it to all GPUs of the node (Section 4.2). This subsection compares the load-back of upstream SGLang with the asynchronous KV fetching of Evolving Infra. Experimental Setup. We use the setup of Appendix D.5: the Claude Code trace with 126 concurrent agents, GLM-5.2 on 36 GB300 GPUs, fixed 4P5D split, and deduplicated host memory (Appendix A.5). The router uses cache-aware routing for prefill nodes and round-robin for decode nodes in both runs, and only the engine data plane differs. Upstream SGLang broadcasts the KV to the GPUs of the node with NCCL collectives, which share the GPUs with the prefill computation. Evolving Infra moves the KV between GPUs with their copy engines over NVLink while the request waits in the queue, and its decode nodes write Table D.5: Asynchronous KV load-back. We score minutes 30 to 85 of each run, and each configuration runs once. Results. With the same routing, the asynchronous load-back of Evolving Infra cuts the idle GPU time of prefill nodes from 23.6% to 14.4% and achieves 1.12 the throughput of upstream SGLang (Table D.5). Mean and P95 TTFT drop by 23% and 24%, and E2E latency by 18% and 21%, although Evolving Infra serves 15% more uncached prompt tokens per second. TPOT stays within 3%. In upstream SGLang, the fetch delays prefill substantially. prefill node must load the fetched KV into GPU memory before the layers that read it can run, and the NCCL broadcast of this KV shares the GPUs with the prefill computation. As result, 93% of its prefill iterations wait more than 10 ms before they start, and waiting for the load-back alone takes up to 8% of the prefill GPU time, about 0.3 for each iteration that consumes fetched KV. These waits add to the queueing delay of every request that fetches its prefix (Section 3.3). Fetches on decode nodes. The same runs show why the decode nodes of Evolving Infra only write to the pool (Section 4.2). In upstream SGLang, decode node also loads reusable KV from its host memory, and the whole batch of the node waits for the load. Decode iterations that start while load-back is in flight leave the GPUs idle 58.7% of the time, with mean gap of 82 ms before the forward, about 19 times the mean TPOT of 4.4 ms, against 6.9% for the other decode iterations. Such iterations are rare (0.5% of decode iterations), but each one stalls every request on the node. Fetches between prefill nodes. prefill node may receive request whose prefix KV resides in the host memory of another prefill node. The node then fetches this KV into its own host memory over RDMA (Section 4.2). We profile these fetches in the run without online phase-split adaptation (Figure 8b) from minute 30 to minute 85. As Figure D.3 shows, the fetch time grows almost linearly with the number of fetched tokens. Each token carries 54.6 KB of KV, and the RDMA transfer reaches about 52 GB/s for large fetches. fetch of 64K128K tokens therefore takes 129 ms at the median. Most fetches are much smaller. For the 92% of fetches with fewer than 16K tokens, the median fetch time is 7 ms. Evolving Infra starts the fetch as soon as the request arrives at the prefill node that serves it. The fetch therefore overlaps with the queueing delay of the request, i.e., the time from this arrival to the start of its prefill. The median queueing delay is 0.72.2 s, at least 3.9 times the median fetch time for every fetch size. fetch that starts only when the prefill begins would instead add its full time to the TTFT.
